questions.prompt: An LTI system has input \(x(t)\), impulse response \(h(t)\) and output \(y(t)=h(t)\ast x(t)\). In the frequency domain, what does this convolution become?
options: An addition: \(Y(s)=H(s)+X(s)\)
A convolution again: \(Y=H\ast X\)
A multiplication: \(Y(s)=H(s)\cdot X(s)\)
A division: \(Y(s)=X(s)/H(s)\)
questions.explanation: Convolution in time becomes multiplication in the (Laplace/Fourier) frequency domain: \(Y=H\cdot X\). That is why filters are easiest to understand in the frequency domain: each frequency component of the input is just multiplied by H at that frequency.

questions.prompt: How is the frequency response \(H(j\omega)\) of an LTI system related to its impulse response \(h(t)\)?
options: \(H(j\omega)\) is the derivative of \(h(t)\) with respect to \(\omega\)
\(H(j\omega)\) is the Fourier (Laplace) transform of \(h(t)\), i.e., \(H(s)\) evaluated on the imaginary axis \(s=j\omega\)
\(H(j\omega)=h(t)\) evaluated at \(t=\omega\)
They are unrelated: one is for sinusoids and the other for impulses
questions.explanation:
\(H(s)=\int h(t)e^{-st}\ dt\) (the Laplace transform), and \(H(j\omega)\) is that function evaluated at \(s=j\omega\). The impulse response and the transfer function are two descriptions of the same system.
The other options are not valid relationships.

questions.prompt: A filter has \(|H|=0.5\) at 1 kHz and \(|H|=0.1\) at 3 kHz. The input is the sum of a tone of amplitude 2 at 1 kHz and a tone of amplitude 2 at 3 kHz. What is the amplitude of the 3 kHz tone at the output?
questions.explanation:
Each input frequency is multiplied by the filter's gain at that frequency. 3 kHz tone: \(2\times 0.1=0.2\). The 1 kHz tone becomes \(2\times 0.5=1\). The tones do not interact because the system is linear.
Common mistake: using the 1 kHz gain (0.5) for both tones.

questions.prompt: An LTI system has impulse response \(h(t)=200\cdot e^{-t/2\ \mathrm{ms}}\cdot u(t)\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Using \(H(0)=\int h(t)dt\), what is its DC gain?
questions.explanation:
At \(\omega=0\ (s=0)\) the transform integral reduces to \(H(0)=\int_{0}^{\infty}h(t)\ dt\): the area under the impulse response.
\(\int_{0}^{\infty}200e^{-t/2\ \mathrm{ms}}\ dt=200\times 2\ \mathrm{ms}=0.4\). So the DC gain is 0.4.
Common mistake: using \(h(0)=200\) as the gain.

questions.prompt: A system has impulse response \(h(t)=(1/\tau)e^{-t/\tau}u(t)\) with \(\tau=0.5\ \mathrm{ms}\). Using \(H(j\omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}h(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt=(1/\tau)/(1/\tau+j\omega)\), what is |H| at \(f=500\ \mathrm{Hz}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega=2\pi\cdot 500=3141.6\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(1/\tau=2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
\(|H|=2000/\sqrt{2000^{2}+3141.6^{2}}=2000/3724.1=0.537\).
Equivalently \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\) with \(\omega\tau=1.571\), so \(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+2.467}=0.537\). Common mistake: using f instead of \(\omega\ (\omega\tau=0.25\) gives 0.970).
questions.figure_alt: Single-pole magnitude response with its corner near 318 hertz and a marked point at 500 hertz.

questions.prompt: A single-pole filter has \(H(jf)=1/(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{kHz})\). The input is the sum of a 1 kHz tone of amplitude 2 and a 10 kHz tone of amplitude 1. What are the output tone amplitudes?
questions.explanation:
\(|H(1\ \mathrm{kHz})|=1/\sqrt{1+1^{2}}=0.7071\) ⇒ \(2\times 0.7071=1.414\).
\(|H(10\ \mathrm{kHz})|=1/\sqrt{1+10^{2}}=1/\sqrt{101}=0.0995\) ⇒ \(1\times 0.0995=0.0995\).
• '1 and 0.091' uses \(1/(1+f/f_{c})\) instead of \(1/\sqrt{1+(f/f_{c})^{2}}\): gains of 0.5 and 0.091.
• '2' wrongly assumes the passband tone at the corner is unattenuated; at \(f_{c}\) the gain is 0.707.
• '1' for the 10 kHz tone ignores the filter entirely.
questions.figure_alt: Asymptotic and exact magnitude of a single-pole filter with a 1 kilohertz corner.

questions.prompt: A system is an ALL-PASS network: \(|H(j\omega)|=1\) at every frequency, but its phase is not a linear function of \(\omega\). A signal made of several sinusoids passes through it. What can happen to the waveform?
options: Nothing: equal magnitude at all frequencies guarantees an identical waveform
Only the overall amplitude can change, by a common factor
New frequencies appear, since the phase is non-linear
The shape can change, because different frequencies are delayed by different amounts of time, even though each tone keeps its amplitude
questions.explanation:
A waveform's shape depends on the relative phases of its frequency components as well as their amplitudes. If \(\angle H\) is not proportional to \(\omega\), the tones are shifted by different times and add up differently. The all-pass network keeps each tone's amplitude but can still distort the waveform ('phase distortion'). Only a linear phase (a pure delay) preserves the shape.
• Equal magnitudes alone do not guarantee an undistorted waveform.
• Amplitudes of the individual tones are unchanged, so it is not a uniform amplitude scaling.
• An LTI system never creates new frequencies.

questions.prompt: A low-pass filter has \(H(jf)=1/(1+jf/1\ \mathrm{kHz})\). The input is \(x=4+3\cos(2\pi\cdot 1\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot t)+2\cos(2\pi\cdot 10\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot t)\). What is the RMS value of the steady-state output? (Tones at different frequencies contribute to mean-square power additively; a DC term contributes its value squared.)
questions.explanation:
Output components: DC: \(4\times H(0)=4\). 1 kHz: \(3\times 0.7071=2.121\) peak. 10 kHz: \(2/\sqrt{101}=0.199\) peak.
Mean square \(=4^{2}+(2.121^{2})/2+(0.199^{2})/2=16+2.25+0.0198=18.27\).
\(RMS=\sqrt{18.27}=4.274\).
Common mistakes: adding peak amplitudes (6.3), or dividing the DC term by \(\sqrt{2}\ (DC\) is already its own RMS value).

questions.prompt: Which statement about \(H(s)\) and \(H(j\omega)\) of a stable LTI system is correct?
options: \(H(j\omega)\) describes the transient response and \(H(s)\) describes the steady state
\(H(j\omega)\) and \(H(s)\) are different functions with no mathematical relationship

\(H(j\omega)\) is \(H(s)\) evaluated on the imaginary axis; it gives the steady-state response to sinusoids, while \(H(s)\) also describes inputs of the form \(e^{st}\) with a decaying or growing real part
\(H(j\omega)\) is only defined for \(\omega>0\), and the response at \(-\omega\) is unrelated to it
questions.explanation:
Setting \(s=j\omega\) in \(H(s)\) gives the frequency response: the eigenvalue of the system for sinusoidal (periodic) complex exponentials, hence the steady-state sinusoidal response. The general \(H(s)\) (any \(s=\sigma+j\omega\)) gives the response to est, which includes transient behavior.
• The roles are reversed in the first wrong option.
• They are the same function on different parts of the complex plane.
• For real systems \(H(-j\omega)=H(j\omega)*\), so negative frequencies carry no new information; they are related.

questions.prompt: Preview of mechanical LTI models. A mass on a spring with damping has \(H(j\omega)=\dfrac{1}{k-m\omega^2+jb\omega}\) from force to position, with \(m=1\ \mathrm{kg}\), \(b=4\ \mathrm{N\,s/m}\) and \(k=100\ \mathrm{N/m}\). What is \(|H|\) at \(\omega=10\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), in m/N?
questions.explanation:
At \(\omega=10\), \(k-m\omega^2=100-100=0\): the spring and mass terms cancel and only damping is left, \(|H|=1/(b\omega)=1/40=0.025\ \mathrm{m/N}\). This is the resonance peak, 2.5 times the static compliance \(1/k=0.01\).
• \(1/k=0.01\) is the DC value.
• \(1/\sqrt{100^2+40^2}\) forgets the \(-m\omega^2\) term.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude of a lightly damped mass-spring system: flat at low frequency, a resonance peak near 10 rad/s, then falling 40 dB per decade.

questions.prompt: Preview of feedback errors. A tracking loop's closed-loop response is \(H(j\omega)=\dfrac{1}{1+j\omega/50}\). The reference is \(r(t)=\cos(20t)\). The tracking error is \(e=r-y\), with frequency response \(1-H\). What is the amplitude of the steady-state error?
questions.explanation:
\(1-H=\dfrac{j\omega/50}{1+j\omega/50}\). At \(\omega=20\): \(\dfrac{|j0.4|}{|1+j0.4|}=0.4/1.077=0.371\).
• \(1-|H|=1-0.928=0.072\) subtracts magnitudes, but y lags r, so the error depends on the phase difference too.
• 0.4 ignores the denominator.

questions.prompt: Preview of dynamic errors in feedback. An ideal closed-loop system would have \(H=1\), but a real one has \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega/\omega_{c})\). At a frequency \(\omega=0.2\omega_{c}\), by what percentage is the MAGNITUDE of the gain below 1? (error \(=(1-|H|)\times 100\%\))
questions.explanation:
\(|H|=1/\sqrt{1+0.2^{2}}=1/\sqrt{1.04}=0.98058\).
Magnitude error \(=(1-0.98058)\times 100\%=1.942\%\).
Note the phase error \((-\tan^{-1}\ 0.2=-11.3^{\circ})\) is also significant. Common mistake: answering 20% (confusing the ratio \(\omega/\omega_{c}\) with the error). For small \(\omega/\omega_{c}\) the magnitude error is only about \(\tfrac{1}{2}(\omega/\omega_{c})^{2}=2\%\), because the magnitude depends on the SQUARE of the ratio.
questions.figure_alt: Single-pole closed-loop magnitude with a marked point at 0.2 omega_c, slightly below 0 dB.
